title: Can animals count, wait and plan?

summary.text: Hide five yellow balls behind one screen and two behind another. In tests like this, a chick only a few days old, who has never been taught about numbers, goes to the screen hiding more. How can a mind with no number words know which pile is bigger? You will test your own sense of 'how many', and your own patience, the way scientists test chicks, bees, crows and a parrot named Alex. Scientists agree that many animals tell more from less. They still argue about whether any of them truly count or plan tomorrow.
summary.art: A fluffy yellow chick standing between two cloth screens, one screen with five yellow balls peeking out on one side and two balls on the other, with a child watching through a gap.

intro.hook: I will show a card for one second. It has three dots. How many did you see? Now a card with nine dots. How many now? Which answer came without counting?
intro.text: Most people know three at once, and do not need to count. With nine dots, you start to guess. Bees, chicks, fish and crows seem to have the same sort of quick feeling for 'how many'. They have no number words at all. In this unit you will find out how far your own quick feeling goes. Then you will see how scientists test the same thing in animals who cannot answer us.
intro.art: A child's hand lifting a paper card with three black dots for a moment, while a bee hovers near a window and a chick peeps from a box.

outcomes: I can explain what number sense is, and give true examples from chicks, fish, bees and a parrot.
I can run a fair dot-flash test and find where my own at-a-glance counting stops.
I can explain why telling 8 from 9 is harder than telling 4 from 8, which scientists call the ratio effect.
I can explain the difference between a number sense and counting.
I can describe how waiting for more food was tested in crows, cuttlefish and children, and why trust matters.
I can explain how scientists tell a clever habit from real planning, using the simplest-explanation rule.
I can explain how a very small brain can still handle numbers.

terms.meaning: A quick feeling for 'how many' or 'which is more', without counting and without number words.
terms.example: A chick goes to the bigger pile of balls.
terms.art: A chick looking at two piles of balls, one big and one small.

terms.meaning: Knowing a small number of things at one glance, without counting them one by one. People usually can do it up to about four.
terms.example: You see three dots on a die and know it is three.
terms.art: A die showing three dots with the number 3 appearing beside it.

terms.meaning: Saying or marking one number for each thing, in order, and knowing that the last number tells how many there are.
terms.example: Touching five bananas and saying one, two, three, four, five.
terms.art: A finger touching each of five bananas in a row.

terms.meaning: How many things there are in a group. Scientists use this word when they test animals.
terms.example: Three dots and five dots have different numerosity.
terms.art: Two cards, one with three dots and one with five dots.

terms.meaning: A way to compare two numbers by dividing one by the other. 4 and 8 have a ratio of 1 to 2.
terms.example: 6 beans against 12 beans is a ratio of 1 to 2.
terms.art: Two small bowls of beans, six in one and twelve in the other.

terms.meaning: Holding back from taking a small reward now, so you can get a bigger one later. Scientists also call it delay of gratification.
terms.example: Leaving one raisin so you can have two in a few minutes.
terms.art: A child with one raisin in front of her, looking at a clock.

terms.meaning: Choosing what to do now because of what you will need later.
terms.example: Packing a school bag the night before.
terms.art: A crow hiding a nut under a leaf while a sunrise is drawn on the horizon.

terms.meaning: A hiding place where an animal stores food for later. As a verb, to cache means to hide food this way.
terms.example: A jay hides acorns in the ground.
terms.art: A jay burying an acorn in soft soil.

terms.meaning: The part of a test that stays the same, so you can see whether the one thing you changed made the difference.
terms.example: Testing the same beans with and without a cloth cover.
terms.art: Two identical setups side by side, one with a cloth cover and one without.

terms.meaning: A rule for animal tests: if a plain habit or a trick explains what an animal did, check that first before saying the animal planned or counted.
terms.example: A dog sits because she smells the treat, not because she knows the word.
terms.art: A magnifying glass over a dog who is sniffing a hand.

terms.meaning: Giving an animal human thoughts and feelings that the evidence does not show.
terms.example: Saying a crow 'is laughing at us' because she tilts her head.
terms.art: A cartoon crow wearing glasses, crossed out with a red line.

terms.meaning: Picturing yesterday or tomorrow in your mind. Scientists argue about which animals can do it.
terms.example: Imagining tomorrow's breakfast while you go to sleep.
terms.art: A child in bed with a thought bubble showing a plate of idli.

explanations.concept: Number sense: knowing 'more' without number words
explanations.description: Number sense is old and shared. Chicks only a few days old go to the bigger group of objects they were raised with. Fish choose to join the bigger shoal. Honeybees, crows and monkeys also tell small numbers apart. Human babies a few months old stare longer when the number of dots changes. None of them has number words, so the feeling for 'how many' comes first, and the words come later. A chick checking two piles is a scientist's best sign that the feeling is built into a living body. Scientists test it by hiding food or objects and seeing which pile the animal picks.
examples: A chick only three or four days old walks to the screen hiding more balls, not fewer.
A fish joins the bigger group of fish in a tank.
A six-month-old baby looks longer when 8 dots change to 16.
explanations.art: A chick, a fish, a bee and a baby, each beside a small group and a large group, with an arrow towards the larger one.
explanations.definition: Number sense is a quick feeling for how many things there are, or which group has more, without counting and without number words.

explanations.concept: Subitising: small numbers at a glance
explanations.description: Look at three coins on a table. You do not count them, you just know there are three. With seven coins, your eyes and mind jump around and you guess or count. In your Dot Flash test, you found where your own at-a-glance knowing stops. Grouping helps a lot. Six dots in two rows of three are easy, because your mind sees two threes. Scientists think this fast sense helped animals judge the size of a rival group or a food pile in a hurry, when counting was too slow.
examples: Seeing the three dots on a die at once.
Knowing two people at the gate without counting.
Reading a dice pattern of six as two groups of three.
explanations.art: A die with six dots in two rows, a ring drawn around each row of three.
explanations.definition: Subitising means knowing a small number of things at one glance without counting. People can usually do it for about one to four things.

explanations.concept: The ratio effect: why 8 and 9 are hard to tell apart
explanations.description: Telling 4 from 8 is easy, and so is 16 from 32, though the difference there is much bigger. Both have a ratio of 1 to 2. Telling 8 from 9 is hard, because the ratio is close to 1. The same pattern shows up in fish, bees, monkeys, crows and in people. Fei Xu and Elizabeth Spelke showed it in 2000 with babies six months old. They told 8 dots from 16 dots, but not 8 from 12. Our quick sense of number is a blurry estimate, and it gets blurrier as numbers grow.
examples: Telling 6 beans from 12 beans at a glance is easy.
Telling 14 beans from 16 beans at a glance is hard.
Six-month-old babies tell 8 dots from 16, but not 8 from 12.
explanations.art: Two pairs of dot cards, one pair of 4 and 8 labelled easy, one pair of 8 and 9 labelled hard.
explanations.definition: The ratio effect means that two groups are easier to tell apart when one is many times bigger, and harder when they are close. It depends on the ratio, not on the difference.

explanations.concept: Counting is more than a number sense
explanations.description: Rochel Gelman and Randy Gallistel studied how children learn to count. They said counting follows rules. Say the numbers in the same order every time. Give one number to each thing, no more. The last number you say tells how many. A number sense is a feeling and counting is a method. Irene Pepperberg's grey parrot Alex, who lived from 1976 to 2007, could say how many objects were in a group, up to about six. In 2005, Pepperberg and Jesse Gordon reported that Alex also had a way of saying 'none'. Alex is among the best-known animals shown to use number words.
examples: Alex the parrot said 'four' when shown four keys.
A child touching each toy and saying the numbers.
A bee judging 'about three' with no counting steps at all.
explanations.art: A grey parrot looking at a tray of four keys, with a woman writing in a notebook beside him.
explanations.definition: Counting means giving one number to each thing, in a fixed order, and knowing the last number tells how many. Number sense does not need any of these steps.

explanations.concept: Bees and numbers: landmarks, none and adding
explanations.description: In 2008, Marie Dacke and Mandyam Srinivasan trained honeybees to fly down a tunnel with stripes on the walls. A reward waited after a fixed number of stripes, up to four. The bees found it even when the stripes were spaced differently. In 2018, Scarlett Howard and her team taught bees to pick the card with fewer dots. When shown a card with no dots, the bees treated 'none' as the smallest number. In 2019, a team led by Howard taught bees that one colour meant 'add one' and another meant 'take one away'. Scientists agree the bees did something that depends on number. They argue about what it is.
examples: Bees found the reward after the third stripe, though the stripes were far apart.
Bees picked a blank card over cards with dots when asked for the fewer.
Bees added or subtracted one dot after seeing a colour.
explanations.art: A honeybee flying down a tunnel with four stripes on the wall and a small sugar dish after the third stripe.

perspectives.who: Researchers who ran the bee tests
perspectives.explanation: The bees used the number of things, and not size, smell or place. So bees have a real number sense, and can learn rules about it, including that none is less than one.

perspectives.who: Cautious scientists, following Lloyd Morgan's rule
perspectives.explanation: Some of the bee results could be explained by a simpler habit, such as 'pick the card that looks emptier'. They ask for more tests that remove every simple trick before calling it adding.

explanations.description: Desert ants walk far across hot sand with no trail to follow, then run straight home. In 2006, Matthias Wittlinger, Rüdiger Wehner and Harald Wolf tested how they know the distance. They added tiny extensions to some ants' legs, like stilts, and cut other ants' legs shorter, like stumps. Ants on stilts took longer steps and walked past the nest. Ants on stumps took shorter steps and stopped before it. So the ants were counting steps, not looking at the sand. With normal legs, one step count is a good measure of distance.
examples: An ant on stilts walks past the nest door.
An ant on stumps stops short of the nest door.
You walking home in the dark by counting your steps.
explanations.art: A desert ant on thin stilts walking past a small nest hole in the sand, with a second ant on short stumps stopping before the nest hole.
explanations.definition: A desert ant keeps track of how far she has walked from her nest by keeping count of her steps, like a pedometer in her nervous system.

explanations.concept: Waiting for more: self-control in people and other animals
explanations.description: Scientists have tested waiting in many animals. In 2014, Friederike Hillemann and her team found crows and ravens waited longer for a food they liked better. In 2021, Alexandra Schnell and her team tested cuttlefish. A cuttlefish waited for a favourite food for up to about one to two minutes, instead of taking a plain one at once. Those who waited longer also learned faster in a second test. Waiting is a choice that needs a picture of a better later. In 2013, Celeste Kidd and her team showed children waited much less when the grown-up had broken a promise before. Waiting depends on trust as well as on willpower.
examples: A cuttlefish waits for live shrimp instead of eating a piece of prawn.
A crow waits for a better nut.
A child waits for two raisins when she trusts the person who promised.
explanations.art: A cuttlefish at the front of a tank with a plain piece of prawn in front and a shrimp behind a clear gate, and a timer drawn above.
explanations.definition: Self-control, also called delay of gratification, is turning down a small reward now to get a bigger one later.

explanations.description: In 2007, Nicola Clayton's team showed that western scrub-jays hid food in the room where they had gone hungry before, not in the room where they always got breakfast. In 2017, Mathias Osvath and Can Kabadayi showed that ravens chose a tool that they would need for a reward later, and used it when the time came. These look like planning. But planning means picturing a future you have not yet met. Scientists disagree about whether a jay or raven pictures tomorrow, or whether an instinct and learned habits can explain the same results.
examples: Jays hid food where they had been hungry before.
Ravens picked a tool, then used it much later.
A child packs her bag the night before school.
explanations.art: A raven picking up a small stick tool and carrying it to a perch, with a locked box in the distance and a moon in the sky.

perspectives.explanation: The birds picked actions that suited a future need, even when nothing in the moment told them to. The simplest fit is that they picture and plan for what they will want.
Picturing a distant future is a special human ability. Birds may be following learned rules or inborn habits. We would need results no simple rule can explain.

explanations.description: A honeybee has about one million neurons, the cells that pass signals in a brain. A person has about 86 billion, which is around 86 thousand times more. Yet bees count stripes and add one. In 2019, Vera Vasas and Lars Chittka built a computer model with only four neurons, and it could estimate how many things it scanned. Scientists have also found neurons in crows that fire for particular numbers. This does not prove bees work like the model. It shows that counting-like jobs may need far fewer neurons than people expect.
examples: A computer model with four neurons estimated a number.
Neurons in a crow's brain fire most for one particular number.
A bee's brain is smaller than a grain of rice.
explanations.art: A honeybee's head next to a grain of rice, and a tiny diagram of four connected dots labelled neurons.

perspectives.explanation: Even a tiny circuit can estimate a number if the bee scans a scene in a smart order. A small brain can use smart methods.
A model that works is not proof that a real bee does the same. Real brains have many more parts that could be involved.

explanations.concept: Number words are a tool people added
explanations.description: People in some communities, such as the Pirahã in Brazil, use very few number words. In 2004, Peter Gordon tested them with lines of batteries and other small objects. They did well when they could match things one to one. They did worse with bigger numbers when they had to remember. In 2008, Michael Frank and his team ran a similar test. Their idea is that number words are a tool, like a ruler, that makes exact numbers possible. Scientists still discuss how many words the Pirahã have, and how much the tool changes thinking.
examples: Matching spoons to bowls needs no number words.
Telling a friend 'seventeen' needs exact number words.
Exact counting stays fast only when you have the words.
explanations.art: A line of batteries on a mat and a second line being laid out beside them, one for one, with no numbers shown.

perspectives.explanation: Number words are a cultural tool. With the tool, exact numbers are easy. Without it, we rely on the quick, blurry number sense and on matching one to one.
Other ideas also matter, such as practice, schooling and memory. They say number words are one part of a bigger story.

explanations.concept: Too much or too little: reading animal minds fairly
explanations.description: In 1894, C. Lloyd Morgan wrote that we should not explain an animal's act as a high mental skill if a simpler skill explains it. That rule is called Morgan's canon. In 1999, the primatologist Frans de Waal added a warning. He named the opposite mistake anthropodenial, which means refusing to see a mind that the evidence shows. Both mistakes are easy. The fair way is to run controls, repeat the test, use a blind helper, and then follow the evidence. In this unit, each result is labelled by what the test really showed.
examples: A dog follows her owner's eyes and not her words, so the test hides the eyes.
A scientist asks a helper who does not know the answer to run the trial.
A crow's trick is tested again with the food hidden from sight.
explanations.art: A scientist with a clipboard behind a one-way screen while a crow chooses between two cups, and a second scientist unaware of which cup holds the food.
explanations.definition: Reading an animal's mind fairly means asking two questions: have I given the animal thoughts the evidence does not show, and have I denied thoughts the evidence does show?

agreed.text: Many animals, from fish to bees to crows, can tell which of two small groups has more, without being taught and without number words.
agreed.evidence: The tests hide food or objects and record which group the animal picks, while controlling for size, smell and position. Teams on several continents found the same.

agreed.text: The ability to tell two groups apart depends on the ratio of the numbers. Close ratios are harder, in other animals and in people.
agreed.evidence: Results with fish, birds, monkeys, babies and adults all show better scores for 4 against 8 than for 8 against 9.

agreed.text: Some animals can wait for a better reward, and waiting is shaped by what they expect to happen.
agreed.evidence: Crows, ravens, cuttlefish and children waited for a better reward in tests with fair controls. Children waited less when a grown-up had broken a promise first.

challenging.claim: Counting needs number words, so only people count.
challenging.who: A view held by many thinkers for a long time.
challenging.for: Exact counting of large numbers needs a list of words in order. Few animals have such a list.
challenging.against: Birds, bees, ants and fish tell numbers apart or track them without any words. Alex the parrot used spoken number words too.

challenging.claim: If a bee passes a number test, she understands numbers like a person.
challenging.for: Bees did tasks that look like adding and having a 'none'.
challenging.against: A task can be done with a simpler rule. Scientists test several rules before calling it understanding. Even then, we know what bees do, and not what it feels like to be a bee.

challenging.claim: A bigger brain always means a smarter animal.
challenging.for: Humans have large brains, and so do dolphins and elephants.
challenging.against: A crow's small brain packs many neurons. A bee's tiny brain does number tasks. Wiring and the way an animal lives matter, not only size.

challenging.claim: Children who wait the longest in the marshmallow test grow up to be the most successful.
challenging.who: Walter Mischel's tests of the 1960s and 1970s, and popular books.
challenging.for: Early studies found a link between waiting time and later results at school.
challenging.against: A 2018 study by Tyler Watts, Greg Duncan and Haonan Quan used a bigger and more varied group. The link was much smaller once family background was counted. Trust and home life shape waiting.

big_questions.q: Bees seem to treat 'none' as a number smaller than one. The Indian mathematician Brahmagupta wrote down the rules for zero in 628 CE. Is zero something people invented, or something minds find?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the empty card meant to the bee, and what 'zero' meant to the mathematicians.

big_questions.q: You know three at a glance but have to count nine. Where does 'knowing' end and 'counting' start?
big_questions.hint: Think about your Dot Flash results, and what changed between 4 and 6 dots.

big_questions.q: If a cuttlefish waits for a favourite food, does she feel wanting, as you do? How would we ever know?
big_questions.hint: Think of what a friend could do to show you they feel something.

big_questions.q: Children waited less when a grown-up had broken a promise. Is that a failure of self-control, or a sensible choice?
big_questions.hint: Think about when taking the raisin now is the clever thing to do.

big_questions.q: A tiny computer circuit of four neurons can estimate a number. Does that make the estimating less real, or more?
big_questions.hint: Think about whether a clever thing must be complicated inside.

big_questions.q: We say a raven 'plans' only if she pictures tomorrow. Do you picture tomorrow, or just do what you have always done?
big_questions.hint: Think about the last time you packed a bag, and what was in your mind.

big_questions.q: Scientists tested bees, ants and crows with tools made for people's tests. What might a test made for a bee look like?
big_questions.hint: Think about what matters to a bee: flowers, colours, smells, distances.

story.title: The Fifth Palm
story.note: A made-up story. Anju, Ammachi, Vishnu and Dr Latha are imagined. Kuttanad in Kerala is real, and so are stingless bees kept in boxes. The science is real. Bees were trained to find a reward after a fixed number of stripes in a tunnel, and they managed up to four. People also know small numbers at a glance, and count larger ones.
text: Anju lived beside a canal in Kuttanad, in Kerala, where the rice fields lie lower than the sea. Her grandmother, Ammachi, kept a row of wooden boxes under the eaves of the house. In the boxes lived stingless bees. They were tiny and black, and they never stung. Each morning they flew out over the paddy fields. Each evening they came home, and Ammachi said she could tell the time by the sound of them.

One afternoon a lady came to see the bees. She was Dr Latha, from the agricultural college. She sat on the step with a cup of tea and told Anju something strange. 'Scientists have made honeybees fly down a tunnel with stripes on the walls,' she said. 'A sugar dish waited after a certain number of stripes. The bees learned to stop at the third stripe, or the fourth. Then the scientists moved the stripes closer, or farther apart. The bees still stopped at the same number.'
'They counted?' said Anju.
'Something like counting,' said Dr Latha. 'The number stayed the same when everything else changed. But the bees managed only up to four stripes. After that, they got muddled.'
Anju thought about it for days. She did not know it yet, but she was about to need it.

The next week the monsoon came hard. On Thursday, school let out early, because the sky had turned the colour of a bruise. Anju walked home along the bund, the narrow path that runs beside the canal. Her cousin Vishnu, who was twelve and very sure of himself, walked ahead of her with his umbrella.
'I know the way blindfolded,' said Vishnu.

Normally you could not miss the turning. There was a red pump house at the corner, and a blue gate just past it. But today the rain came sideways, and the light went out of the day. The pump house was a grey shape. The blue gate was gone, torn off in the storm. All along the path, coconut palms stood in a row, black against the grey. They all looked exactly the same.
'It is the next one,' said Vishnu.
'No,' said Anju. 'We have passed the bridge. I think there are more.'

'It is five palms after the bridge,' said Vishnu. 'I can see them from here. One, two, three, four, five.' He pointed his umbrella at the dark line of trunks, and said it quickly, with a flick of his hand. 'That one, with the broken top, is the fifth. Turn here.'

Anju looked at the trunks. Rain ran into her eyes. In the dark, she could not tell which trunk was the first. She remembered Dr Latha on the step. The bees managed up to four stripes, the scientist had said. After that, even a bee gets muddled.

She remembered something else too. When she glanced at three marbles, she knew they were three. When she glanced at nine, she had to count. Her eyes were good with a few things and poor with many. Vishnu had glanced at a row of palms in the dark and said five. He had not counted. He had only felt it.
'Stop,' said Anju. 'Let us count them properly. We will touch each one. Go back to the bridge.'
'That is silly,' said Vishnu. 'It is just a row of trees.'
'Then it will not take long,' said Anju.

They went back to the wooden bridge. Anju put her hand flat on the first palm after it. The trunk was rough and wet, with a bend in it. 'One,' she said. She moved to the next. 'Two.' Then 'three'. Then her hand found a palm with a broken top, a stump against the sky. 'Four,' she said.
'Four?' said Vishnu. 'That is the fifth one. I said so.'

'It is the fourth,' said Anju. 'I touched every one. Come and feel.' She walked on, past the broken top. A few steps farther, her hand found another trunk, hidden behind a curtain of fallen fronds. 'Five,' she said. 'The turn is here.'
Vishnu stood very still. 'I did not see that one,' he said slowly. 'The leaves had hidden it. I did not count at all. I just felt five.'
'A feeling is a good start,' said Anju. 'But it was too quick for this many.'

They went on together. Anju touched the fifth palm, and under her feet the path bent left, just as it should. A light was swinging at the end of it. It was Ammachi, with a hurricane lantern, standing at the door with her sari pulled over her head.
'You are late, and wet,' said Ammachi. 'How did you find the turn? There is no blue gate any more.'
'We counted palms,' said Anju. 'Vishnu guessed. I counted.'
Ammachi laughed so hard that her lantern shook. 'The bees knew that,' she said. 'Come in. They are all home already, every one of them, safe in their boxes.'

That night, while Vishnu dried his hair, Anju sat at the window and listened to the hum from the boxes. She thought of the storm, and the black palms, and of what had stayed the same while everything else changed. The colour of the light was gone. The gate was gone. The path was mud. But the palms were still five, and the turn was still after the fifth.
story.epiphany: When looks change, the count can stay the same. A glance is quick and works for a few things, but for more things you have to count.
ask: When is counting a better guide than looking?
Why might it be easy to know three things at a glance, and hard to know eight?
How could you test whether a bee follows the number of stripes, or the colour of the stripes?
Can a feeling for 'how many' be wrong? How would you check it?
