A girl pressing her palm against a wet coconut trunk as she counts, her cousin holding an umbrella behind her.
A grandmother holding a hurricane lantern at the door, with wooden bee boxes under the eaves.

roots.context: You tested how many things you can know at a glance, and you met chicks, bees, ants and a parrot who handle numbers without number words. Now we ask what this says about number itself, and about you.

deep_truth.truth: You knew three dots at a glance, and chicks and bees tell small numbers apart too. None of them needs number words for that. A feeling for 'how many' comes first, and words only make it exact.
deep_truth.habit: We think of number as something people make with words and schools, so a mind without number words must have no sense of number. This mixes up the tool for saying numbers with the sense of how many.
deep_truth.evidence: Your Dot Flash scores were right up to about four dots and then became guesses. Chicks went to the bigger pile, bees found the third stripe, and desert ants walked a number of steps home.

three.who_am_i: You are an animal with an old, quick sense of 'how many' that you share with a chick and a bee.
three.what_is_life: Living beings need to know how much food, how many steps and how long to wait, so a feeling for number is part of staying alive.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is full of groups that can be more or fewer, and minds of very different kinds notice that.

roots.thread: Before anything can be counted, there is none. Then there is one. Then there are two, three and many. A bee that picks the blank card over a card with dots has met none. A chick that picks five over two has met many. Counting is one way minds meet the One becoming the many. The number words came later, and they make the feeling exact.

teachings.teaching: As paraphrased: in the beginning there was only Being, one without a second. Being thought, 'Let me become many.'
teachings.link: Counting starts with one and moves to many. Your sense of number is the mind meeting that step.

teachings.teaching: As paraphrased: the Tao gives birth to One. One gives birth to Two. Two gives birth to Three. Three gives birth to all things.
teachings.link: The first numbers come in a line, one after another, which is how a bee sees stripes and how you touch palms.

teachings.teaching: Brahmagupta wrote down rules for calculating with zero, as a number in its own right.
teachings.link: Bees in a 2018 test treated an empty card as the smallest number. People wrote rules for zero more than a thousand years ago.

science.text: Chicks, fish, bees and many other animals tell small numbers apart without being taught or having number words.
Whether this is counting like ours, or a different kind of knowing, is still argued over.

other_view.who: Some psychologists, following C. Lloyd Morgan (1894)
other_view.view: Do not call it number sense if a simpler cue, such as the size, smell or space taken by the pile, explains the result. 'Number' may just be our word for several simple cues working together.

practice.title: One look, then count
practice.say: Look around the room and pick a group of things, such as pots on a shelf or birds on a wire. Look at them for one breath only. Now close your eyes. Ask yourself how many there were. Notice if the answer came by itself, or if you had to guess. Open your eyes and count. Smile whether you were right or not.
practice.kid: Pick a group of things. Look at them for one breath. Close your eyes. How many were there? Now open your eyes and count.

ask: When you know 'three' without counting, where does the knowing come from?
Is a number something in the world, or something minds make? What would a bee say?
If a chick can tell more from less, what else might you share with her?
roots.art: A child at a window with her eyes closed and a thought bubble holding three dots, while a bee and a chick look at the same three dots from outside.

games.title: Wait or Take? The seed game
games.context: This is a game of choices. Each round you choose to take one seed now, or wait to win three. You find out when waiting pays and when it does not.

setup.art: A bowl of seeds as the bank, and each player with their own nest bowl and a plate for waiting seeds.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and seeds. Set up the bank, your nest and your waiting plate.

setup.art: A hand placing one seed on the waiting plate, and a second hand taking a seed into the nest.
setup.caption: 2. Choose in secret: take one seed now, or wait.

setup.art: A face-down card being turned over to show Safe on one side and Thief on the other.
setup.caption: 3. Turn over the top card to see if waiting paid.

printables.title: 20 two-sided cards in two decks of 10: a Meadow deck and a Riverbank deck, each with the result on the back
30 seed tokens (the start of the bank, to be topped up with dry beans or rice grains)

rules: Cut out the cards and keep the Meadow cards and the Riverbank cards in two separate piles. A helper picks one pile, shuffles it, and puts it face down. The helper does not say which is more trustworthy. Alone, shuffle the pile and do not look at the backs.

Put the seed tokens in a big bowl in the middle. This is the bank. Add dry beans or rice grains until it holds about 50 seeds for each player, so the bank does not run out. Each player has a nest bowl and a waiting plate.
In each round, every player chooses in secret. Take means you move one seed from the bank into your nest. Wait means you move one seed from the bank onto your waiting plate.

Then turn over the top card. If it says Safe, every player who waited moves three seeds from the bank into their nest, and the seed on the waiting plate goes back to the bank. If it says Thief, the seed on the waiting plate goes back to the bank, and the waiting player gets nothing.
Take always keeps its one seed. Wait may win three seeds or nothing.
After 10 rounds, count the seeds in your nest. Then play 10 rounds with the other pile.
The player with the most seeds after both piles wins. If players tie, they share the win. Alone, try to beat 20 seeds in total.

flow.do: Cut out the 20 cards and the 30 seeds. Fill the bank bowl with dry beans or rice grains to about 50 seeds for each player. Keep the two piles apart. Give each player a bowl for a nest and a plate for waiting seeds. Put the bank in the middle.
flow.say: Cut out the cards and seeds. Put the seeds in the middle. Each player gets a bowl and a plate.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Cut out the seeds. Set up your bowl and plate.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Wait or Take game. You set up the cards, seeds and bowls.

flow.do: Shuffle one pile, face down, without showing the backs. Play the first three rounds. After each card, say what you chose and why.
flow.say: Choose in secret: take one seed, or wait. Then I turn over the card. Did waiting pay?
flow.kid: Take one seed, or wait. Then turn the card.
flow.context: In this step, you play the first three rounds of the game.

ask.q: After three cards, do you want to keep waiting, or take? Why?
good: Waiting won twice, so I will keep waiting.
Thieves came twice, so I will take.
I need more cards to know.

flow.do: Play the other seven rounds of the first pile. Keep count of how many Safe and Thief cards you have seen. Count the seeds in each nest.
flow.say: Keep playing. Try to remember how many Safe cards and how many Thief cards there have been.
flow.kid: Keep playing. Count the Safe and Thief cards.
flow.context: In this step, you finish the first pile and count the seeds.
flow.parent: Players who count the cards learn what is coming. This is the same thing a crow does when she learns which place is safe. A deck of 10 has exactly 8 of one kind and 2 of the other.

flow.do: Play the second pile for 10 rounds. Add up the seeds from both piles. Then ask which pile was the safer place to wait, and when you changed your choice.
flow.say: Now the other pile. Do you want to wait or take? How will you know?
flow.kid: Play the other pile. Add your seeds.
flow.context: In this step, you play the second pile and add up your total.

check.q: In a place where Thief cards come most of the time, which choice scores best?
check.why: In a place with many Thief cards, waiting often loses its seed. Taking one seed each round scores steadily. A good player changes the choice when the place is not safe. Children in a 2013 study also waited less when an adult had broken a promise before.

flow.parent: Meadow has 8 Safe cards and Riverbank has only 2. Waiting every round in Meadow gives 24 seeds, and taking every round gives 10. In Riverbank, waiting gives only 6. Talk about how you decided, and when you stopped trusting a place.

experiments.title: Dot Flash: how many can you know at a glance?
experiments.question: How many dots can you know at one glance, without counting? Does arranging the dots in groups make it easier?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Up to how many dots will you get right in one second? Will neat groups of dots be easier than scattered ones? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every card is shown for the same time, about one second. The dots are black, the same size, on white cards. You never count out loud or point. The cards come in a mixed-up order, and each card is shown twice. Only the number of dots and the pattern change.

materials.item: 11 white cards cut from thick paper, each about 10 centimetres by 15 centimetres (one is a spare for practice)
a black marker
a plain sheet of paper to cover each card, and a pencil
the results table

experiments.record: For each card, write the number of dots and whether the answer was right on try 1 and try 2. Then circle the first row where you made a mistake. Compare the scattered six with the six in two rows of three.
experiments.context: In this test, you flash cards with dots for one second each, and find out how many dots you can know at a glance.

setup.art: A table with ten white cards and a black marker, one card showing three scattered dots.
setup.caption: 1. Draw dots on ten cards: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9 scattered, a 6 in two rows of three, and an 8 as two groups of four.

setup.art: The back of a card with the number of its dots written small in the corner.
setup.caption: 2. Write the number of dots on the back of each card.

setup.art: A parent holding a card under a plain sheet, ready to lift the sheet for a moment, with a child watching.
setup.caption: 3. Hold a card face down under a plain sheet. Lift the sheet and say 'one'.

setup.art: A child saying a number aloud with her hands folded, while the parent marks a tick on a table.
setup.caption: 4. The child says the number at once, without counting. Write a tick or a cross.

flow.do: Show your child the blank cards. Ask for a guess about how many dots they will see in one second, and why. Write the guess at the top of the table.
flow.say: We will flash cards with dots for one second each. You say how many dots you saw. What is the biggest number you think you can know without counting? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess the biggest number of dots you can know at a glance. Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Dot Flash test. You guess before you test.

ask.q: Why do you think dots in groups will be easier, or harder?
good: Groups are easier because I can see small parts.
Spread dots are harder because I lose my place.
I am not sure, we can test it.

flow.parent: Write the guess down. Do not correct it. Any guess with a reason is a good start.

flow.do: Draw the dots on the ten cards. Spread the scattered dots in no pattern, with no lines or shapes. Draw one card with 6 dots in two rows of three, and one with 8 dots as two groups of four. Write the number on the back of each.
flow.say: Draw the dots with the marker. Make them all the same size. Scatter them, with no lines. Write the number on the back of each card.
flow.kid: Draw the dots on the cards. Write the number on the back.
flow.context: In this step, you make the cards for the test. The dots are all the same size.
flow.parent: Scatter the dots so no shape appears. If dots touch, they count as one blob and the test is spoiled. Keep the same size for every dot.

flow.do: Practise with one spare card. Hold it face down under the sheet. Lift the sheet, say 'one', and lay it back. Your child says the number. Practise twice.
flow.say: Watch the sheet. When I lift it, I will say one. Then I cover the card again. Say the number you saw. Do not count with your fingers.
flow.kid: Watch the card for one second. Say the number. Do not count.
flow.context: In this step, you practise the flash, so the real test is fair.
flow.parent: One second is very quick. Say 'one' at the speed of a normal word. If the card is visible for longer than that, the test is not fair.

flow.do: Shuffle the cards. Flash each card once and tick or cross the answer in the table. Shuffle again and flash each card a second time. Do not show the cards from small to big.
flow.say: Here comes the first card. Ready? Say the number. Good. Here is the next.
flow.kid: Say the number you saw. Do not count.
flow.context: In this step, you run the real test, two times through the ten cards.

check.q: Why do we shuffle the cards instead of going from 2 up to 9?
options: So the child cannot guess from the order
check.why: If the cards go from small to big, the child can guess the next number without looking. A mixed order makes the answers come from the dots, not the order.

flow.parent: If your child gets every card right, even 9, the flash was probably too long. Try again with 12 and 15 dots. If your child is upset by wrong answers, remind them that guessing is the point.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Find the first row where mistakes begin. Compare the scattered six with the six in two rows. Ask your child to write what they think, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Look at the table. Where did the mistakes start? Compare the two sixes. Which was easier? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Where did you start to make mistakes? Which six was easier?
flow.context: In this step, you look at the results and say what they show.

ask.q: Where did your mistakes begin? What was different about the cards with mistakes?
good: After four dots.
When there were more dots, I could not hold them all.
The dice six was easier because I saw two threes.

ask.q: The two sixes had the same number of dots. Why was one easier?
good: I could see two threes.
The dots were in groups.
Grouping lets me know a big number as small parts.

flow.parent: Most children are right on 2, 3 and 4 dots, and begin to guess at 5, 6 or 7. The grouped six and eight are usually easier than the scattered ones. This is called subitising, and grouping uses it twice. Say the word after your child has said what they saw.
flow.think: A chick only a few days old goes to the bigger of two groups of balls. What does that tell you about number words?

experiments.title: Which Pile Is Bigger? The ratio test
experiments.question: Four pairs of piles each differ by 6 beans. Does your child tell them apart equally well, or do the pairs with the closer sizes get harder?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Pairs: 6 and 12, 12 and 18, 18 and 24, 24 and 30. In every pair, one pile has exactly 6 more beans. Which pair will be hardest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every pair is shown for about one second. Each pair is tested six times, with the bigger pile on the left half of the time and on the right half of the time. The beans in each pile are spread inside the same size circle. Only the number of beans changes. The difference between the two piles stays 6.

materials.item: 90 dried chickpeas or rajma beans
5 small katoris or cups
2 sheets of paper, each with a circle about 15 centimetres wide drawn on it by tracing a plate
a clean dishtowel or cloth to cover the piles
a coin, to decide left or right
the results table and a pencil

experiments.safety: Dried beans can choke small children. Keep them away from children under five, and do not let anyone put them in their mouth or nose.
experiments.record: For each pair, write how many of the six tries were right. Then draw a bar for each pair, with the height showing the number right.
experiments.context: In this test, you flash two piles of beans for one second and your child points to the bigger. The difference between the piles is always 6, but the pairs get closer in size.

setup.art: A kitchen table with five katoris holding 6, 12, 18, 24 and 30 chickpeas, counted in rows of six.
setup.caption: 1. Count out five piles into katoris: 6, 12, 18, 24 and 30 beans.

setup.art: Two sheets of paper with circles on them, each holding a spread pile of chickpeas, with a cloth over them.
setup.caption: 2. Spread one pile on each sheet, inside the circle. Cover both with the cloth.

setup.art: The cloth being lifted for one second while a child looks, and the parent with a stopwatch drawn in thought.
setup.caption: 3. Lift the cloth, say 'one', and cover the piles again.

setup.art: A child pointing to the left sheet, while the parent writes a tick on a table.
setup.caption: 4. The child points to the bigger pile. Write a tick or a cross.

flow.do: Show the five katoris you will fill. Explain that in every pair, one pile has exactly six more beans. Ask which pair your child thinks will be hardest, and why. Write the guess down.
flow.say: In every pair, one pile has six more beans than the other. Which pair do you think will be hardest to tell apart? Why?
flow.kid: Which pair of piles will be hardest? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Which Pile Is Bigger test. You guess before you test.

ask.q: All the pairs differ by six. Does that make them equally hard? Why or why not?
good: Yes, because the gap is the same.
No, because six is small when the piles are big.
I do not know, so let us test.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. A good guess has a reason, even if it turns out wrong.

flow.do: Count the beans into five katoris: 6, 12, 18, 24 and 30. Count in rows of six, which is easier. Put the katoris in a row, smallest to biggest. Keep this out of your child's sight if you can.
flow.say: Let us count out the piles. We count in rows of six. Six, twelve, eighteen, twenty-four, thirty. Check that each pile is right.
flow.kid: Count out 6, 12, 18, 24 and 30 beans. Use rows of six.
flow.context: In this step, you prepare the five piles for the test.
flow.parent: Piles must be exact. Count twice. If a bean rolls away, count again. Use the same size of bean for every pile.

flow.do: Practise once. Spread the 12 pile on one sheet and the 18 pile on the other, inside the circles. Cover both. Lift the cloth for one second, then cover again. Ask your child to point to the bigger one.
flow.say: I will lift the cloth for one second. Point to the pile with more beans. Do not count. Just point.
flow.kid: Look for one second. Point to the bigger pile.
flow.context: In this step, you practise the flash, so the real test is fair.
flow.parent: Toss the coin before each try. Heads: the bigger pile goes on the left. Tails: on the right. Do this while your child's eyes are closed.

flow.do: Test the pairs in this order: 12 and 18, then 24 and 30, then 6 and 12, then 18 and 24. For each pair, run six tries. Before each try, toss the coin, set the piles, and cover them. Flash for one second. Write a tick or a cross.
flow.say: Eyes closed, please. Now open. Point to the bigger pile. Good. Eyes closed again for the next.
flow.kid: Eyes closed. Open. Point to the bigger pile.
flow.context: In this step, you run the real test, six tries for each of the four pairs.

check.q: Why do we toss a coin to decide which side the bigger pile goes on?
options: So the child cannot guess that the bigger pile is always on one side
So the coin gets a turn
check.why: If the bigger pile were always on the left, a child could point left and score full marks without looking. The coin makes the side random, so the score comes from judging the piles.

flow.parent: Mix the order of the pairs, so a child cannot get used to one gap. If a pair is clearly easy, still do all six tries. Each pair must have the same number of tries.

flow.do: Fill in the 'right out of 6' column. Draw a bar for each pair on the back of the sheet. Ask your child what they think, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Look at your bars. Which pair was hardest? The gap was six every time. What do you think made the hard pair hard?
flow.kid: Which pair was hardest? Why, when the gap was always six?
flow.context: In this step, you draw the results and say what they show.

ask.q: In every pair the gap was six. Why were some pairs harder than others?
good: Six is a big part of 12 but a small part of 30.
When the piles are big, six more looks like a tiny bit.
It depends on how many times bigger one pile is.

flow.parent: Most children do well on 6 and 12, do well on 12 and 18, and begin to guess on 24 and 30. This is called the ratio effect. A pair like 6 and 12 has a ratio of 1 to 2. A pair like 24 and 30 has a ratio of 4 to 5. A ratio close to 1 is harder. A caution for your child: the closer pile also looks more crowded, and that is a clue. Real scientists control for this by changing the size of the objects. You can try it by using bigger beans in the smaller pile.

experiments.title: The Waiting Test: what helps you wait for more?
experiments.question: Which helps most when you wait for more: seeing the treat, hiding it under a cup, or hiding it and doing a puzzle?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. On which day will you wait the longest: treat in sight, treat under a cup, or treat under a cup while you do a puzzle? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Each day uses the same treat, the same offer, the same place and the same time of day. The offer is always 1 raisin now, or 2 raisins if you wait 3 minutes. Only the way of waiting changes. The three ways are shuffled, so that practice cannot explain the result.

materials.item: 6 raisins, or 6 pieces of another small treat your child loves
a plate and a steel cup that hides the plate
a timer, such as a phone
a drawing puzzle or a colouring page
3 slips of paper to draw the order from a bowl
the results table

experiments.safety: Check that your child has no allergy to the treat, and only use treats they can chew safely. Do not run the test when your child is hungry, tired or upset.
experiments.record: Each day, write how many minutes your child waited, up to 3, and whether they got one treat or two. At the end, line up the three days and compare.

schedule.what: Draw the order from the bowl and play the first round.
Play the second round at the same time of day.
Play the third round and then compare the three days.

experiments.context: In this test, your child gets a choice of one treat now or two later, and tries three different ways of waiting on three different days.

setup.art: A plate with two raisins and a plate with one raisin side by side, with a timer between them.
setup.caption: 1. The offer: one raisin now, or two if you wait three minutes.

setup.art: A child sitting at a table looking at the raisins, with a timer showing three minutes.
setup.caption: 2. Way 1: wait with the raisins in sight.

setup.art: A steel cup upside down over the plate while the child sits at the table.
setup.caption: 3. Way 2: wait with the raisins hidden under a cup.

setup.art: A child drawing a picture while a cup hides the plate on the table behind her.
setup.caption: 4. Way 3: hide the raisins and do a drawing puzzle while you wait.

flow.do: Explain the game. Your child may stop and take the one raisin at any time, and there is no scolding. Draw the order of the three ways from the bowl and write it down. Ask which day your child will wait longest, and why.
flow.say: This is a game, not a test of you. You may take one raisin any time. If you wait three minutes, you get two. We will try three ways of waiting on three days. Which way do you think will be easiest? Why?
flow.kid: A game of waiting. Take one raisin anytime. Wait three minutes for two.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Waiting Test. You explain the game and guess.

ask.q: What do you think will help you wait the longest, and why?
good: Hiding it, because I will not keep looking.
Doing something fun, because I forget about it.
Looking at it, because it reminds me why I am waiting.

flow.parent: The test is only fair if you always keep your promise. If your child waits, give two at once, with thanks. Never use the result to say a child is good or bad at waiting.

flow.do: Day 1. Play the way you drew first. Put one raisin on a plate for now and two on another for later. Start the timer. Stop at three minutes or when your child takes the one raisin. Write the minutes waited.
flow.say: Here is one raisin now. Or you wait three minutes for two. I start the timer now. You can stop any time.
flow.kid: One raisin now. Or wait for two. You choose.
flow.context: In this step, you play the first round of the waiting game.
flow.wait: Leave it for a day. Play the second round at the same time tomorrow.
flow.parent: Do not talk about the raisins while your child waits. Stay near, and keep your face calm. If your child sings or talks to themselves, write that down.

flow.do: Day 2. Play the way you drew second. Use the same offer, place and time of day. Write the minutes waited.
flow.say: Same game as yesterday, but with a different way to wait. One now, or two if you wait three minutes. You decide.
flow.kid: Same game. A new way to wait. You choose.
flow.context: In this step, you play the second round of the waiting game, with a different way of waiting.
flow.wait: Leave it for a day. Play the third round at the same time tomorrow.

flow.do: Day 3. Play the last way. Use the same offer, place and time of day. Write the minutes waited. Keep the promise: if your child waits, give two.
flow.say: Last round. One now, or two after three minutes. You decide.
flow.kid: Last round. You choose.
flow.context: In this step, you play the third and last round of the waiting game.

flow.do: Line up the three days in the table. Ask your child what they think, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Look at the three days. Which way helped you wait most? What did you do in your head to help?
flow.kid: Which way helped you wait most? Why?
flow.context: In this step, you look at the three rounds and say what helped most.

ask.q: Which way helped most, and what do you think was going on in your head?
good: Hiding the raisins helped, because I could not see them.
Drawing helped, because I stopped thinking about the raisins.
Looking did not help me.

ask.q: Would you wait as long if I had broken my promise last week? Why or why not?
good: No, because I would not trust you.
I would take the one now, in case.
Waiting only makes sense if I trust you.

flow.parent: Many children wait longest when the treat is hidden and they are busy. Some wait longest when they look at it. Both are fine. The last question links to a 2013 study by Celeste Kidd and her team: children waited much less when an adult had broken a promise to them first.

activities.title: String Puzzle: look first or try first?
activities.context: In this activity, you pull the right string to bring a toy, and notice whether you look first or try first. Ravens have been given a similar puzzle.

materials.item: 2 strings or ribbons in different colours, each about 80 centimetres long
a small toy or an empty matchbox
a heavy book
a table or a long tray
a pencil and paper

setup.art: A table with two coloured strings laid side by side, one leading to a toy at the far end and the other leading to a heavy book.
setup.caption: 1. Tie one string to the toy. Tie the other to a heavy book.

setup.art: The same strings crossing once in the middle so the left near end leads to the right far end.
setup.caption: 2. Round 2: cross the strings once in the middle.

setup.art: The strings crossing twice and looping around a pencil in the middle of the table.
setup.caption: 3. Round 3: cross the strings twice and loop them around a pencil.

flow.do: Tie the toy to one string and the heavy book to the other. Lay the strings side by side on the table, with the toy and the book at the far end. Leave the near ends within your child's reach. Ask which string will bring the toy, and how they know.
flow.say: Two strings lead away from you. One is tied to the toy. The other is tied to a heavy book. Which string should you pull to bring the toy?
flow.kid: Which string brings the toy? How do you know?
flow.context: This is the first step of the String Puzzle. You set it up and guess.
flow.parent: Hide the toy's string by changing the order from child to child. Do not point.

flow.do: Cross the strings once in the middle of the table, so the left near end leads to the right far end. Ask your child to pull the one they choose. Watch what they do before they pull, and write it down.
flow.say: The strings cross now. Pull the one you think brings the toy.
flow.kid: The strings cross. Pull the string you choose.
flow.context: In this step, you play round 2, with crossed strings.

ask.q: What did you do in your head before you pulled?
good: I followed the string with my eyes.
I traced it with my finger.
I just guessed.

flow.parent: Write down if your child looked first, traced with a finger, or pulled at once. Do not hint. If they pull the wrong string, say nothing, and let them try again.

flow.do: Cross the strings twice and loop one string around a pencil. Ask your child to pull. Watch if they trace with their eyes or finger before pulling.
flow.say: This one is harder. The strings cross twice, and one goes around the pencil. Pull the string you choose.
flow.kid: A harder puzzle. Pull the string you choose.
flow.context: In this step, you play round 3, with the strings crossed twice.

check.q: When a child follows a string with her eyes before pulling, which best describes what she does?
options: She plans the pull in her mind before acting
check.why: Looking first and then pulling the right string at once means the answer was worked out before the action. Trying one string and then the other is trial and error. Both are ways of solving a problem.

flow.parent: Many children trace the string with a finger or with their eyes. This is a way of thinking before acting.

flow.do: Ask your child which round they solved by looking first and which by trying. Tell them that ravens have been tested with a similar puzzle.
flow.say: In 1995, the scientist Bernd Heinrich gave ravens a piece of meat hanging on a string. Some ravens pulled up the string and held it with a foot, again and again, until the meat reached them. Do you think they worked it out first, or learned it step by step? How could we tell?
flow.kid: Did you look first, or try first? How would you test a raven?
flow.context: In this step, you compare your way of solving with how ravens were tested.

ask.q: How could we tell if a raven worked it out first, or learned it step by step?
good: See if she does it right the first time she sees a new puzzle.
Change the puzzle and see if she still solves it.
Watch if she tries wrong ways first.

flow.parent: Scientists do disagree on this. Some see insight, a mind working out the answer. Others see trial and error, or an inborn habit. Heinrich saw some ravens solve the puzzle quickly and took this as insight. Other scientists say the ravens may have learned it step by step, so the question is still open.

activities.title: Stilt Steps: be a desert ant
activities.context: In this activity, you walk like a desert ant. You count your steps out, then walk the same number of steps home with very long steps and very short steps, and see where you land.

materials.item: masking tape or chalk
a long room, passage or terrace, at least 4 metres long
a ruler or a tape measure
paper and a pencil

setup.art: A child standing at a tape line at one end of a passage, with a second tape line at the other end.
setup.caption: 1. Stick a tape line at the start and one at the far end.

setup.art: A child walking with normal steps to the far line, with a number floating above each foot.
setup.caption: 2. Walk to the far line with normal steps and count them.

setup.art: A child walking back taking giant steps and landing far past the start line.
setup.caption: 3. Walk back with giant steps, the same number of steps.

setup.art: A child shuffling back with tiny steps and stopping far short of the start line.
setup.caption: 4. Walk back with tiny steps, the same number of steps.

flow.do: Stick a start line and a far line about 4 metres apart. Ask what will happen if your child walks home with the same number of steps, but much longer ones.
flow.say: Desert ants find home by counting steps. I want you to be a desert ant. If you take the same number of steps home, but much longer steps, where will you land? Why?
flow.kid: Same number of steps, but longer. Where will you land? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of Stilt Steps. You guess before you try.

ask.q: If you take longer steps but the same number of steps, will you stop short, at the line, or past it? Why?
good: Past it, because longer steps go farther.
Past the start line.
I think I will go too far.

flow.parent: Write the guess down. The ant counts steps and not how big they are, so longer steps carry her past the nest.

flow.do: Your child starts at the start line, and walks to the far line with normal steps, counting each one. Write down the number of steps. Mark the far line with their toes.
flow.say: Walk to the far line with your normal steps. Count each step. Say the number at the end.
flow.kid: Walk to the far line. Count your steps.
flow.context: In this step, you count the normal steps from the start to the far line.
flow.parent: Do not let your child look back. If the steps differ by one or two on a repeat, that is normal. Use the same number for the two trials.

flow.do: From the far line, your child walks back with the same number of steps, but as long as they can. Mark where they stop. Measure how far they are from the start line.
flow.say: Now walk home with the same number of steps. Make each step a giant stride. Look straight ahead and stop when you have counted them all.
flow.kid: Walk home with the same number of giant steps.
flow.context: In this step, you walk back with giant steps, like an ant on stilts.
flow.parent: Cover the start line with a sheet of paper after the first walk, so your child cannot see it. Use a dry, clear floor with no loose rugs, and no running. Measure the distance past the start line. Stilts made the ants overshoot in the same way.

flow.do: From the far line, your child walks back with the same number of steps, but as tiny as possible. Mark where they stop. Measure how far short of the start line they are. Ask what they think, saw and why.
flow.say: Now the same number of steps, but tiny shuffles. Where will you stop? Then say what you saw and why.
flow.kid: Same number of steps, but tiny. Where do you stop?
flow.context: In this step, you walk back with tiny steps, like an ant on stumps.

ask.q: What does this tell you about how the ants know the distance home?
good: They count their steps, but not how long each one is.
Their steps tell them the way.
They do not measure distance by looking.

flow.parent: In 2006, Matthias Wittlinger, Rüdiger Wehner and Harald Wolf glued pig bristles to some desert ants' legs as stilts, and cut others shorter as stumps. Ants on stilts overshot the nest and ants on stumps stopped short. The ants counted their steps and could not tell the steps were different. A real ant also looks at the sun, so your result is a model of the idea, not the same test.

activities.title: Fair or Fishy? Check an animal genius claim
activities.context: In this activity, you read four made-up claims about clever animals, and decide which to trust, and what more you would ask.

materials.item: a pencil and paper

setup.art: Four claim cards laid in a row on a table, each with a small drawing of a dog, a parrot, a crow and a bee.
setup.caption: 1. Read the four claims.

setup.art: Three boxes labelled Trust, Trust a little and Ask for more tests, with the cards being sorted into them.
setup.caption: 2. Sort the claims into three boxes.

setup.art: A child writing a question on a sticky note and placing it on a claim card.
setup.caption: 3. Write one question that would make the weakest claim stronger.

flow.do: Read the four made-up claims aloud. Claim A: A dog barks the right number of times when his owner asks for 2 plus 3. The owner stands next to him and knows the answer. Claim B: A parrot says 'four' for four keys in many trials. The person who sets the tray does not know the answer. The keys change in size and colour. Claim C: A video shows a crow dropping stones in a tube once. No other tries are shown. Claim D: Two labs in different countries taught bees to pick the card with fewer dots. Both labs tested empty cards. In both, the helper who set the cards did not know the right side.
flow.say: Here are four claims about clever animals. They are made up. Listen to each one. For each, think about how we could be fooled.
flow.kid: Listen to four claims. How could we be fooled?
flow.context: This is the first step of Fair or Fishy. You read four made-up claims about clever animals.
flow.parent: Read each claim slowly and ask what could explain it other than number.

flow.do: Sort the claims into Trust, Trust a little and Ask for more tests. Ask why for each one.
flow.say: Put each claim in a box. Say why. What could fool us in this one?
flow.kid: Sort the claims. Say why for each one.
flow.context: In this step, you sort the claims by how much you trust them.

ask.q: Which claim needs the most checking, and why?
good: A, because the owner may be giving small signals.
C, because one video is one try.
A, because the dog might read the owner's face.

ask.q: Which claim would you trust most, and why?
good: B, because the helper did not know the answer.
D, because two labs got the same result.
B or D, because they had controls.

flow.parent: Claim A is like Clever Hans, a horse who seemed to count. The owner may give tiny signs. Claims B and D have a blind helper and use controls. Claim D also repeats in another lab. Claim C is one try, so more tests are needed.

flow.do: Pick the weakest claim. Write one question, or one change to the test, that would make it stronger. Share it.
flow.say: Pick the claim you trust least. What one change would make the test fair?
flow.kid: Pick the weakest claim. How would you fix the test?
flow.context: In this step, you write the one change that would make the weakest test fair.

check.q: Which change makes a dog's counting test fairer?
options: A helper who does not know the answer asks the question from behind a screen
The dog is given more treats
check.why: If the person who knows the answer cannot be seen, the dog cannot read small signs from them. A blind helper and a screen remove that clue, so the dog's answer is more likely to come from number.

activities.title: Crow's Choice: which pile does she pick? (if a bird visits)
activities.context: In this activity, you offer a crow, myna, pigeon or squirrel two small piles of food over several days, and see which pile the visitor goes to first. Try it if a bird or squirrel visits your balcony, terrace or garden.

materials.item: 2 small plates or lids of the same size
unsalted puffed rice, bits of plain bread or boiled rice
a pencil and paper
a coin

activities.safety: Wash your hands after touching the food or plates. Keep your distance from the bird and never try to touch or catch her. Feed only a little, and only during the test days.

schedule.what: Set the two plates out with 2 pieces and 6 pieces. Toss the coin for the sides. Note which pile the visitor goes to first.
Do it again. Toss the coin for the sides.
Do it again. Toss the coin for the sides.
Do it again. Toss the coin for the sides.
Do it once more, then count which pile won on how many days.

setup.art: Two small plates on a balcony rail, one with two pieces of puffed rice and one with six.
setup.caption: 1. Put 2 pieces on one plate and 6 on the other.

setup.art: A coin being tossed above the balcony rail, to decide which plate goes on the left.
setup.caption: 2. Toss a coin to decide the sides.

setup.art: A crow landing on the rail near the plate with six pieces, while a child watches from the doorway.
setup.caption: 3. Watch from a distance and write which pile she goes to first.

flow.do: Set out the two plates on a balcony rail or terrace wall, 30 centimetres apart. Put 2 pieces on one and 6 on the other. Toss a coin to decide the sides. Step back and watch. Note which pile the visitor goes to first.
flow.say: Two plates, one small pile and one big pile. We toss the coin to decide the sides. Then we watch from far away. Which pile will she go to first? Why?
flow.kid: Two plates. Watch from far away. Which pile first?
flow.context: In this step, you set out the plates and watch which pile the visitor goes to first.
flow.wait: Repeat each day for five days.

ask.q: Which pile do you think the visitor will go to first? Why?
good: The big one, because she sees more food.
The closer one.
I do not know.

flow.parent: Only count the first choice. If no one visits in 20 minutes, pick up the food and try again on another day. Birds are shy, so be patient and stay still.

flow.do: On the last day, count the days the bigger pile was first. Count the days the smaller pile was first. Ask what the result shows. Ask what else could explain it.
flow.say: Let us count up the five days. How many times did she choose the big pile first? What else could explain it?
flow.kid: Count the days. Which pile won most often?
flow.context: In this step, you count up the five days and say what the result shows.

ask.q: If the bird often picks the bigger pile, does that prove she counts? What else could she be using?
good: She could be using how big the pile looks.
She could be using smell.
She might just go to the pile nearer to her.

flow.parent: Five tries is very few. Scientists use many more. The bigger pile also looks bigger and smells stronger, so this cannot prove number sense. Treat it as a first look.

challenges.title: Design a Number Test for a Crow
challenges.problem: A crow visits the window every morning. You want to find out whether she can tell which of two piles of food has more, and not only which looks bigger or smells stronger. Design a fair test.
constraints: You cannot use number words with the crow.
The test must work with food you already have at home.
The test must be hard to solve using only size, smell, position or your own hints.
Plan at least 10 tries, in a mixed-up order, over at least two days.

materials.item: paper and a pencil
a few small pieces of puffed rice or bread

challenges.context: In this challenge, you design a fair test for a crow's sense of number, using what you learned about controls.

setup.art: A child sketching two plates with different piles on paper, with arrows pointing to the things that could give the answer away.
setup.caption: 1. List the clues the crow might use besides number.

setup.art: A sketch of two plates with a screen between them and a coin for deciding sides.
setup.caption: 2. Draw your test, with a coin for the sides.

setup.art: A family member acting as the crow, pointing to a pile while the child writes a tick.
setup.caption: 3. Test your plan on someone in your family.

flow.do: Ask your child to list the things a crow could use to pick the bigger pile, other than number. Examples: how big the pile looks, the smell, the side, a sign from you. Write them down.
flow.say: A crow could pick the bigger pile in other ways. What other clues could she use? Write them all down.
flow.kid: List the clues a crow could use besides number.
flow.context: This is the first step of the challenge. You list the tricks that could fool you.

ask.q: What are some things a crow might use instead of number?
good: How big the pile looks.
The smell.
Which side is nearer.
My face or my hand.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw a plan that removes each clue they listed. Examples: use a coin for the side, hide yourself, use bigger pieces in the smaller pile. Write how many tries and how they will be scored.
flow.say: Now draw a test that fixes each clue. How will you choose the sides? Where will you stand? How many tries?
flow.kid: Draw a test that fixes each clue.
flow.context: In this step, you draw a plan that removes each clue.
flow.parent: Look for a coin for the sides, a screen or distance for the helper, and varied piece sizes for size.

flow.do: Test the plan on a family member who acts as the crow and cannot see your hints. Count the tries they get right. Find one clue they used that you forgot.
flow.say: A family member plays the crow. Can they find the bigger pile without counting? What clue did they use?
flow.kid: Test your plan on a family member.
flow.context: In this step, you test the plan on a family member acting as the crow.

check.q: A crow always picks the pile on the left. What does this most likely show?
check.why: If the side decides her choice, the test does not show number sense. A coin to choose the side breaks that clue.

flow.do: Improve the plan using what the family member used. Write the final plan in four lines.
flow.say: Fix the one clue you missed. Write your final plan in four lines.
flow.kid: Fix the clue you missed. Write your final plan.
flow.context: In this step, you improve the plan and write it out.

general: Two plates with different numbers of pieces, and the crow goes to the bigger.
Use a coin to choose the side.
Count how many tries the bigger pile wins.
creative: Make the pieces in the smaller pile bigger, so both piles weigh and look the same.
Hide the piles behind two screens and let the crow see how many go behind each, like the chick tests.
Ask a helper who does not know the answer to set up each try.
Use the same test for a street dog or a pigeon.
challenges.your_turn: Invent a number test for an animal you often see, such as a crow, a squirrel, a street dog or a pet. Write how you would control size, smell and position, and how many tries you need.

worksheets.title: Animal Number Detective (core)

items.p: What is number sense?
opts: A quick feeling for how many, without counting or number words
items.why: Number sense is the quick feeling for 'how many' or 'which is more'. Chicks, fish and bees have this feeling, though they have no number words.

items.p: A chick has seen only yellow balls since she hatched. Five balls go behind one screen and two behind another. Which screen does she go to?
items.why: In tests, chicks only a few days old went to the screen hiding more balls. This shows that the sense of 'more' is there very early in life.

items.p: Honeybees can learn to stop at the third stripe in a tunnel, even when the stripes are spaced farther apart.
items.why: True. Marie Dacke and Mandyam Srinivasan found that bees kept the same count when the spacing changed, up to about four stripes.

items.p: Knowing a small number of things at one glance, without counting, is called ____.
items.why: Subitising is the quick knowing of small numbers. People are usually good at it up to about four things.

items.p: Which pair of piles is hardest to tell apart at a glance?
items.why: 8 and 9 have a ratio close to 1, so they look almost the same. 6 and 12, and 10 and 20, each have a ratio of 1 to 2, which is easy.

items.p: Counting and number sense are exactly the same thing.
items.why: False. Number sense is a quick feeling. Counting is a method with rules: say the numbers in order, one for each thing, and the last number tells how many.

items.p: Desert ants find their way home by keeping count of their ____.
items.why: Ants with glued-on stilts walked past their nest, and ants with shortened legs stopped short. So they counted steps, not distance.

items.p: Explain how you could find out how many dots a person can know at a glance, without letting them count.
items.a: Flash cards with different numbers of dots for about a second, in a mixed-up order, and ask for the number. The first number where answers become guesses shows the limit.
items.why: A strong answer says the cards are shown very briefly, in a random order, and the person does not count. It then says where mistakes begin.

items.p: Why is it unfair to test a dog's counting if the owner knows the right answer and stands in front of the dog?
items.a: The dog may be reading tiny signs from the owner, such as a look or a small movement, instead of counting.
items.why: A strong answer says the owner could be giving a hidden clue. A fair test uses a helper who does not know the answer.

items.p: Match each animal to what happened in a number test.
pairs: stopped at the right stripe in a tunnel
walked past the nest on stilts
said the number of objects on a tray
chose the bigger group of balls
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each test shows number being used without number words, except the parrot, who used spoken number words.

items.p: Sort each one by whether you can do it at a glance or need to count.
items: 6 dots in two rows of three
items.a: as given
items.why: People know small numbers, and neat groups of small numbers, at a glance. Larger scattered numbers need counting.

items.p: Meera tosses a coin before each try. When it lands heads, the bigger pile goes on the left. In 20 tries, heads came 9 times. On how many tries was the bigger pile on the right?
items.why: 20 take away 9 is 11. The bigger pile was on the right on the 11 tries when the coin landed tails.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? A fish joins the bigger shoal. A chick picks the bigger group. A bee stops at the third stripe. A child learns to read.
items.a: A child learns to read. The other three use a quick sense of number.
items.why: Fish, chicks and bees all show number sense without number words. Learning to read is a different skill.

items.p: Draw 8 dots in two ways: one way that is quick to know at a glance, and one way that is hard. Write why.
items.a: Eight dots as two groups of four in neat rows, and eight dots scattered. The groups are quick because you see two small groups.
items.why: A strong drawing shows groups of four for the easy one and a random scatter for the hard one, with a reason about groups.

items.p: Why do scientists show the left or right side at random in a number test?
opts: So the answer cannot be found from the side alone
items.why: If the bigger pile were always on the same side, an animal could score well just by going to that side. Random sides force the answer to come from the piles.

items.p: A bigger brain always means a better sense of number.
items.why: False. A honeybee has about a million neurons and still handles number tasks. What a brain does depends on how it is wired, not only on its size.

worksheets.context: This sheet checks the main ideas of the unit: what number sense is, how it is tested, and how big a number you can know at a glance.

worksheets.title: Ratios, Waiting and Fair Tests (stretch)

items.p: Two piles have a ratio of 1 to 2. Which pair is it?
items.why: 20 is 2 times 10, so the ratio of 10 to 20 is 1 to 2. The other pairs are closer.

items.p: Babies six months old told 8 dots from 16 dots, but not 8 from 12. What does this show?
opts: The ratio matters, and 1 to 2 is easier than 2 to 3
items.why: Fei Xu and Elizabeth Spelke found that babies used the ratio. 8 to 16 is 1 to 2, which is far from 1. 8 to 12 is 2 to 3, which is closer.

items.p: Telling 20 from 30 is as easy as telling 20 from 21.
items.why: False. 20 and 30 have a ratio of 2 to 3, and 20 and 21 have a ratio very close to 1. The closer the ratio is to 1, the harder.

items.p: The rule that says not to explain an animal's act by a high skill if a simpler skill fits is called Morgan's ____.
items.why: C. Lloyd Morgan wrote this rule in 1894. It asks us to check the simpler explanation first.

items.p: Giving an animal human thoughts that the evidence does not show is called ____.
items.why: Anthropomorphism gives animals human traits without evidence. The opposite mistake is anthropodenial, which denies a mind the evidence does show.

items.p: A news story says, 'Dog adds numbers.' Write two questions you would ask before you believe it.
items.a: Who set the test, and did they know the right answer? Was the test repeated many times and in a mixed-up order?
items.why: Strong questions ask about hidden clues, a helper who does not know the answer, repeats, and controls.

items.p: Explain why a small brain does not have to mean a weak sense of number.
items.a: A bee has only about a million neurons, but she can learn the third stripe and even add one. A small circuit of four neurons in a computer model can estimate a number. So the way a brain is wired matters more than its size.
items.why: A strong answer uses the bee or the four-neuron model as evidence and says how a brain is wired matters.

items.p: Put the steps of a fair animal number test in order.
a: List what the animal might use besides number, such as size or smell
Change those things so they cannot help
Ask a helper who does not know the answer to set up each try
Run many tries in a random order
Compare the score with what luck would give
items.why: First you list the clues. Then you remove them. A blind helper removes your own hints. Many random tries make the result trustworthy. Last, you compare with luck.

items.p: Sort each claim by whether it has good evidence or needs more tests.
items: Two labs got the same bee result and the helpers did not know the answer.
A video shows a crow solving a puzzle once.
A dog taps the right number while the owner stares at him.
A parrot gets the number of keys right in many tries set by a blind helper.
items.a: as given
items.why: Repeats, blind helpers and a second lab make a result stronger. One try, or a helper who knows the answer, leave room for tricks.

items.p: Match each test to what it checks.
pairs: One raisin now or two later
A blank card against a card with dots
whether none is treated as a number
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each test is built to show one thing and hide the others.

items.p: Two friends read that bees passed a test where they added one dot.

views.who: Rina, a girl in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: The bee passed the adding test, so she understands maths just like us.

views.who: Karthik, a boy in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: She may have used a simple rule. We need more tests before we say that.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with more? What test would help to decide?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side, gives a reason, and describes a test, such as changing the dots, the colours and the helper.
items.why: Both views fit the facts. A good test removes simple rules, for example by changing the size and colour of the dots.

items.p: Draw a simple picture of the ratio effect. Show a pair of dot groups that is easy to tell apart and a pair that is hard.
items.a: An easy pair such as 4 and 8 dots, and a hard pair such as 8 and 9 dots, labelled easy and hard.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that the easy pair has a ratio far from 1, and the hard pair has a ratio close to 1.

items.p: Suppose a cuttlefish waits 2 minutes, which is 120 seconds, for her favourite food. A child waited 3 minutes for two raisins. How many seconds longer did the child wait?
items.why: 3 minutes is 180 seconds. 180 take away 120 is 60. The child waited 60 seconds longer.

items.p: Children waited much less when a grown-up had already broken a promise. What is the best reading of this?
opts: Waiting depends on trust as well as on willpower
items.why: If the later reward may not come, taking the small reward now is sensible. Waiting works only in a place you trust.

items.p: If an animal waits for a better reward, scientists know exactly what she feels while she waits.
items.why: False. Waiting can be measured, but what it feels like to wait cannot yet be measured in another being.

items.p: Why were stilts and stumps used on desert ants?
opts: To change how long each step was, without changing the number of steps
To keep them off the hot sand
items.why: If ants count steps, longer legs should carry them too far and shorter legs not far enough. That is what happened.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Knowing 3 dots at once. Knowing which pile has more. Counting 9 dots one by one. A chick picking the bigger group.
items.a: Counting 9 dots one by one, because it is a method with steps, not a quick feeling.
items.why: The other three use the quick sense of number. Counting uses rules and steps.

worksheets.context: This sheet goes deeper into the ratio effect, waiting for more, and how to tell a trick from real thinking.

worksheets.title: Zero, Bees and Brains (challenge)

items.p: Rao says, 'Animals have no number words, so they cannot have any sense of number.' Argue for or against, using one animal as evidence.
items.a: Against. A desert ant on stilts walked past her nest, so she counts steps without words. Number sense works with no words.
items.why: A strong answer takes a side, names an animal and a finding, and says why the finding answers Rao.

items.p: A crow picks the pile with more peanuts. Which extra check best shows she uses number and not size?
opts: Use bigger peanuts in the smaller pile, so both piles take up the same space
Use the same peanuts and the same pile size
Give her more time to look
items.why: If the smaller pile has bigger peanuts, the size and the space cannot give away the answer. Only the number is different.

items.p: A raven chooses a tool and uses it hours later. Which result would make 'she planned' hardest to doubt?
opts: She picks the right tool for a task she has never seen before
She uses the tool she always uses
She picks a tool at random
items.why: A new task cannot be solved by an old habit. If she still picks the right tool, planning is a better explanation.

items.p: An animal that fails one number test has no sense of number.
items.why: False. The test may have been unfair or too hard. Scientists try different tests before they decide.

items.p: A game has 10 rounds. Each round you may take 1 seed, or wait. Waiting gives 3 seeds if the round is Safe and 0 if it is Thief. In a deck with 8 Safe and 2 Thief rounds, how many seeds do you get by waiting every round?
items.why: 8 Safe rounds times 3 seeds is 24. The 2 Thief rounds give 0. Waiting every round gives 24 seeds.

items.p: In the same 10-round game, taking 1 seed each round gives 10 seeds. How many more seeds does waiting every round win in the deck with 8 Safe and 2 Thief rounds?
items.why: Waiting wins 24 and taking wins 10. 24 take away 10 is 14 more seeds.

items.p: In a deck with 2 Safe and 8 Thief rounds, which choice scores more over 10 rounds?
items.why: Waiting wins 3 seeds on 2 Safe rounds, which is 6. Taking wins 10. In an untrustworthy place, waiting does not pay.

items.p: Two friends argue about bees and zero.

views.who: Priya, a girl in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: A bee that picks an empty card as 'fewer' knows what zero is.

views.who: Imran, a boy in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: She may only know that 'empty' is less than 'some'. That is not the same as zero in sums.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with more? What would you test to find out?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side, gives a reason, and describes a test, for example whether bees can use none in adding or subtracting.
items.why: Both views have a point. The bees ranked none below one, but sums with zero are a bigger step, so more tests are needed.

items.p: Brahmagupta wrote rules for zero in 628 CE. In 2018, bees treated an empty card as less than one. Does that mean bees invented zero? Explain.
items.a: No. Bees ranked 'none' as less than one, which is an important part of zero. People went further and wrote rules for adding and multiplying with zero. A feeling for none is older than the rules.
items.why: A strong answer separates sensing 'none' from writing rules for zero as a number.

items.p: Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: a hiding place for stored food
the part of a test that stays the same
giving animals thoughts the evidence does not show
how many things are in a group
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These four words are the tools scientists use to talk about animal minds fairly.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Hiding a nut for tomorrow. Packing a bag the night before. Sneezing at pepper. Choosing a tool for a later task.
items.a: Sneezing at pepper, because it is a quick reflex and not a choice made for later.
items.why: The other three are choices made for something later. A sneeze happens at once.

items.p: Sort each one into number sense or counting.
items: Choosing the bigger pile at a glance
Saying one, two, three in order for each toy
A bee picking the card with fewer dots
Knowing the last number you said tells how many
items.a: as given
items.why: Number sense is quick and needs no steps. Counting follows rules that people teach and practise.

items.p: A computer circuit of four neurons can estimate how many things it scans. What can we say?
opts: A small circuit can do some number tasks, but this does not prove that a real bee works this way
items.why: Vera Vasas and Lars Chittka showed a small circuit can work. Whether a real bee uses that circuit is a separate question for more tests.

items.p: Design a quick test for a street dog, who has no number words. Draw the two plates, and write what you would control.
items.a: Two plates with different numbers of biscuit pieces, with a coin for sides. Controls: the size of the pieces, the smell, the side and a helper who does not know the answer.
items.why: A strong design lists the clues the dog could use apart from number and shows how each is removed.

items.p: In a good animal test, the person who sets up each try should always know the right answer.
items.why: False. A person who knows the answer can give small signs without meaning to. A helper who does not know is safer.

items.p: How might number words help us to say big numbers exactly?
opts: Words give each number its own name and place in a list, so we can say 17 and not just 'many'
Words have nothing to do with numbers
items.why: The quick sense of number is blurry for big numbers. Number words let people say exactly how many, as the research with the Pirahã community and others suggests.

worksheets.context: This sheet asks you to argue, design and decide, with bees, crows, zero and small brains.

quiz.p: Which is the best example of an animal using number sense?
opts: A fish joins the larger of two groups of fish
A fish swims in a tank
quiz.why: Choosing the larger group means telling which group has more, which is number sense. Swimming and eating do not need it.

quiz.p: A child tells 3 dots from 4 dots at a glance, but cannot tell 12 from 13. What best explains this?
opts: The quick sense of number is sharp for small numbers and blurry when the ratio is close to 1
The child has not learned maths
quiz.why: Small numbers can be known exactly. Bigger numbers are estimated, and close ratios blur together.

quiz.p: Which pair is the easiest to tell apart at a glance?
quiz.why: 5 and 10 have a ratio of 1 to 2. The other pairs have ratios very near 1, so they are much harder.

quiz.p: Two pairs of bean piles both differ by 6. One pair is 6 and 12. The other is 24 and 30. Why is the 6 and 12 pair easier?
opts: 6 to 12 is a ratio of 1 to 2, which is far from 1
Six beans are easier to see
quiz.why: Ratio matters more than the gap. 24 to 30 is 4 to 5, which is close to 1, so it is harder.

quiz.p: Which of these is counting, and not only number sense?
opts: Touching each toy, saying the numbers in order, and using the last number as the total
Seeing two groups and knowing one is bigger
quiz.why: Counting follows rules: numbers in order, one for each thing, and the last number is the total. Number sense needs none of these.

quiz.p: A cuttlefish waits for a better food instead of taking a plain one. What does this show?
opts: She can hold back a small reward now for a bigger one later
quiz.why: This is self-control. Waiting is a choice, and the tests show she makes it.

quiz.p: Why might children wait less if a grown-up has already broken a promise?
opts: They may think the later reward will not come, so taking now is sensible
quiz.why: Celeste Kidd and her team found that trust changes how long children wait. Waiting pays only in a reliable place.

quiz.p: A horse seems to count by tapping, but only when the owner can see the answer. What should a scientist check first?
opts: Whether the horse is reading small signs from the owner
quiz.why: If the horse is reading hidden signs, number is not needed. A helper who does not know the answer can check.

quiz.p: What does Morgan's canon ask a scientist to do?
opts: Check a simpler explanation before saying an animal used a high skill
Always say animals are as clever as people
quiz.why: C. Lloyd Morgan asked scientists to try the simplest explanation first. Frans de Waal added that we must also not deny a mind that the evidence shows.

opts: Refusing to see a mind or feeling that the evidence shows
Giving animals human feelings with no evidence
quiz.why: Frans de Waal used this word for the opposite of anthropomorphism. Both are mistakes, and the fair way is to follow the evidence.

quiz.p: A honeybee has about a million neurons and still handles number tasks. What does this suggest?
opts: The size of a brain is not the only thing that sets what it can do

quiz.p: Desert ants on stilts walk past their nest. What does this suggest?
opts: They keep count of their steps, and longer steps carry them too far
quiz.why: The ants counted the same number of steps, but each step was longer, so they overshot. That points to step counting.

open_questions.q: Do bees and chicks feel 'three' the way you do?
open_questions.why_open: We can test what they do. Nobody can yet test what it is like to be a bee.

open_questions.q: Is a number sense in animals the same thing as counting?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists define counting in different ways, so the same result is called counting by some and not by others.

open_questions.q: Do any animals picture tomorrow, or do they follow habits and instincts that look like planning?
open_questions.why_open: A hidden habit can look like planning. No test so far rules out every simple explanation for every animal.

open_questions.q: Do fish, crabs and insects wait for more because they want more?
open_questions.why_open: Waiting can be measured, but wanting is a feeling, and nobody can yet measure a feeling in another being.

open_questions.q: How does a brain of a million neurons do number tasks?
open_questions.why_open: A four-neuron model shows it is possible. Nobody knows yet which circuit a real bee uses.

maths.problem: In a pile test, one pair has 6 and 12 beans. Another pair has 24 and 30 beans. Write each pair as a fraction, the smaller pile over the bigger pile, and simplify. Which fraction is closer to 1? What does that tell you about how hard each pair is to tell apart?
maths.answer: 6/12 = 1/2 and 24/30 = 4/5. 4/5 is closer to 1, so the pair 24 and 30 is harder.
maths.explain: 6 over 12 simplifies by dividing both by 6 to get 1 over 2. 24 over 30 simplifies by dividing both by 6 to get 4 over 5. One half is far from 1, and four fifths is close to 1. The closer to 1, the harder to tell apart.
maths.context: In the Which Pile Is Bigger test, every pair differs by 6 beans, but the pairs get closer in size.
maths.why_maths: A fraction shows how close two numbers are in size. The ratio effect depends on that, not on the gap between them.

maths.problem: In a Dot Flash test, Meera got 6 of 6 right on the 2, 3 and 4 dot cards, 4 of 6 right on the 5, 6 and 7 dot cards, and 1 of 4 right on the 8 and 9 dot cards. For each group, write the fraction she got right. Which fraction is the smallest?
maths.answer: 6/6, 4/6 = 2/3 and 1/4. The smallest is 1/4, for the 8 and 9 dot cards.
maths.explain: 6 out of 6 is 1 whole. 4 out of 6 is 2 over 3. 1 out of 4 is 1 over 4. One quarter is less than two thirds, which is less than 1 whole. So the 8 and 9 dot cards were hardest.
maths.context: In the Dot Flash test, you flash cards with 2 to 9 dots and note which answers are right.
maths.why_maths: A fraction of tries right lets you compare groups of cards with different numbers of tries.

maths.problem: In a waiting game, each round you can take 1 seed, or wait. Waiting wins 3 seeds on a Safe card and 0 on a Thief card. A deck has 10 rounds, with 8 Safe and 2 Thief. How many seeds does waiting every round give, and how many does taking every round give? How many more is the waiting?
maths.answer: Waiting gives 24, taking gives 10, so waiting gives 14 more.
maths.explain: 8 Safe rounds times 3 seeds is 24 seeds. 10 rounds times 1 seed is 10 seeds. 24 take away 10 is 14.
maths.context: In the Wait or Take game, you choose each round between taking 1 seed and waiting for a chance at 3.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying shows what each choice earns over many rounds, so you can see when waiting is a better plan.

maths.problem: A child starts the three-minute wait at 5:05 pm. She takes the single raisin at 5:07 pm. How long did she wait? How much of the three minutes was left? At what time would she have got two raisins?
maths.answer: She waited 2 minutes, 1 minute was left, and she would have got two raisins at 5:08 pm.
maths.explain: From 5:05 to 5:07 is 2 minutes. 3 minutes take away 2 minutes is 1 minute. 5:05 plus 3 minutes is 5:08.
maths.context: In the Waiting Test, your child waits up to three minutes for two raisins, or stops early and takes one.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting times tells you exactly how long someone waited, so you can compare the three ways of waiting fairly.

how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, many thinkers said that counting needs words. Animals have no number words, so they could not count. In the 1930s and 1940s, a German scientist called Otto Koehler tested this. He trained birds, including a raven called Jakob and some jackdaws, to pick out a chosen number of marks or food items. He changed the size, shape and place of the things, so the birds could not use any clue except the number. The birds managed small numbers, up to about five or six. Koehler called this 'thinking in unnamed numbers'. Later scientists said he had not controlled every clue, and tested again with better controls. Later, Irene Pepperberg's grey parrot Alex used spoken number words, and Marie Dacke's bees stopped at the right stripe in a tunnel. So words are not needed for number. Words only make big numbers exact.
how_we_found_out.who: Otto Koehler among the first, then Irene Pepperberg, Marie Dacke and many others
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Counting needs number words, so animals cannot sense number. Koehler's birds picked the right number with no words, and later bees, ants and a parrot did too.

playtest: Checked as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, not yet tried at home. Dot Flash needs 11 hand-drawn cards, one second each. The flash is hard to time by hand, so the parent says 'one' while the card is open. If a child gets every card right, use cards with 12 and 15 dots. Which Pile Is Bigger needs 90 dried chickpeas or rajma, counted in rows of six, and about 37 minutes with 24 tries. Beans in a bigger pile also look more crowded, so this cannot prove number sense alone. Keep beans away from children under five. The Waiting Test runs over three days. Check for food allergies, always keep the promise of two raisins, and do not use the result to judge a child. Wait or Take has 20 cards and 30 paper seeds, and needs a bowl of dry beans or rice grains to top up the bank. It is playable alone, with a parent or with friends. A deck of 10 has exactly 8 cards of one kind and 2 of the other. Print the Meadow and Riverbank cards on different colours of paper if you can. Stilt Steps needs a dry passage of 4 metres. Crow's Choice depends on a bird or squirrel visiting, and is not in the core path. Still to settle: the three videos are still to be found, and every activity needs a real try at home. The exact figures for the Pirahã number words are argued over by linguists, so the unit does not give them.
